passages.happening:
The father begins with a long ‘if’. ‘My son, if you accept my words and hide my commandments within you’ (verse 1), if you turn your ear to wisdom, if you call out for insight, ‘if you seek it like silver and search it out like hidden treasure’ (verse 4), then you will find something.

‘Then you will discern the fear of the LORD and discover the knowledge of God’ (verse 5). And the reason is not the son's effort after all: “For the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding” (verse 6). God stores up sound wisdom for the upright and guards the path of those who walk with integrity (verses 7-8).

Then wisdom will come into the son's heart, ‘and knowledge will delight your soul’ (verse 10). ‘Discretion will watch over you, and understanding will guard you’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
In Hebrew the whole chapter reads almost as one long sentence: if you do these things, then you will understand, and wisdom will rescue you, so that you will walk the right way. Several scholars note that it has twenty-two verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, which may be a quiet sign of design.

Silver and hidden treasure meant real value in a world without banks. People buried valuables in the ground or hid them in walls, and mining for silver was hard, patient work in dark tunnels. The picture is about effort. Wisdom rewards those who dig for it.

Hide is the Hebrew word tsaphan, to treasure or store away. In 1:11 the gang used the same word for lying in wait. Here it is turned to good use: storing what is precious.

The chapter holds two things together and does not explain how they fit. Wisdom takes real effort: listening, calling out, searching. And wisdom is finally God's gift. The son seeks, and the LORD gives.
passages.later: Job 28 uses the same picture: ‘Surely there is a mine for silver and a place where gold is refined’ (Job 28:1). Then it asks, ‘But where can wisdom be found, and where does understanding dwell?’ (Job 28:12). And James repeats the promise of verse 6: ‘if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him’ (James 1:5).
passages.asks: People search hard for what they think is valuable. Ask what you dig for most eagerly, and whether wisdom is on that list. And ask God for it, since the chapter says it is his to give.

passages.t: Rescued from crooked men and from the forbidden woman
passages.happening:
Wisdom will protect the son from two dangers. The first is men ‘who leave the straight paths to walk in the ways of darkness’ (verse 13), ‘who enjoy doing evil and rejoice in the twistedness of evil’ (verse 14), ‘whose paths are crooked and whose ways are devious’ (verse 15).

The second is a woman. ‘It will rescue you from the forbidden woman, from the stranger with seductive words’ (verse 16), ‘who abandons the partner of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God’ (verse 17). ‘For her house sinks down to death, and her tracks to the departed spirits’ (verse 18). ‘None who go to her return or negotiate the paths of life’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
These two dangers match the two voices of chapter 1, the gang and Wisdom. The woman introduced here will fill chapters 5 to 7.

The Hebrew uses two words for her: one for a strange woman or outsider, and one for a foreign woman. Some scholars take this literally, as a warning against marrying women of other nations and their gods, a real concern after the exile (Ezra 9 and 10; Nehemiah 13). Others think it means a woman outside one's own marriage, strange to the young man because she belongs to another. Verse 17 supports the second reading. It says she has left the partner of her youth and forgotten the covenant of her God, so she is presented as a married Israelite woman unfaithful to her husband.

Covenant, berit in Hebrew, is the Bible's great word for a binding relationship sealed by promises, used of God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel and David. Here it is used of marriage. A marriage is made before God, with God as witness, so adultery breaks faith with a spouse and with the LORD.

The departed spirits are the rephaim, the weak and shadowy dead in Sheol. Her house is a road that runs downhill into the grave.
passages.later: The prophet Malachi speaks of marriage the same way: ‘the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant’ (Malachi 2:14).
passages.asks: The chapter warns about crooked paths and broken promises. Ask whether there is any path you are on that is slowly bending away from the straight one. And if you are married, ask how you keep your covenant in small and daily ways.

passages.t: The upright will remain in the land
passages.happening:
‘So you will follow in the ways of the good, and keep to the paths of the righteous’ (verse 20).

The chapter ends with two outcomes. ‘For the upright will inhabit the land, and the blameless will remain in it’ (verse 21); ‘but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the unfaithful will be uprooted’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
These verses echo the covenant promises and warnings of Deuteronomy, where living in the land depends on being faithful to the LORD. The land was the inheritance God promised to Abraham and gave through Moses. Wisdom here is not a private skill. It is the way to live securely as part of God's people in God's land.

For readers after the Babylonian exile, when many in Judah had been uprooted from the land and some had come back, these words would have carried the weight of recent memory. Earlier readers would have heard the same themes in the prophets.
passages.later: Moses set the same choice before Israel: ‘For He is your life, and He will prolong your life in the land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers’ (Deuteronomy 30:20). Psalm 37 takes the long view: ‘But the meek will inherit the land’ (Psalm 37:11), and ‘The righteous will inherit the land and dwell in it forever’ (Psalm 37:29). Jesus took up that psalm's promise: “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5).
passages.hard:
Is it true that the upright always remain in the land and the wicked are always uprooted?

Verses 21 and 22 state the covenant pattern: faithfulness leads to a secure life in God's land, and wickedness leads to being cut off. Read as a proverb, this says how things tend to go under God's rule, and how they will finally be set right.

It is not a promise that no righteous person will ever lose a home, or that the wicked never prosper for a time. The Psalms and Job wrestle openly with the wicked who flourish. Faithful Israelites such as Daniel and Ezekiel were carried into exile along with the guilty.

So the proverb is true as a direction and as a final outcome, even when life in the short term seems to say otherwise. It gives no one a reason to look at someone who has lost their home and decide that they must be among the wicked.
passages.asks: The chapter looks to where each path ends. Ask what it would mean to keep walking the paths of the righteous when the short term looks unfair. And ask whether you have ever judged someone's character by their losses, when the Bible says the righteous can lose much too.
